result:
There is a particular quality to rain on a Tuesday afternoon that never makes it into the poetry. Not the thunderstorm, not the slow grey curtain of November, but this: a flat, ordinary drizzle that starts around three o'clock and does not stop. It is the rain of people who are alone in their apartments, who have been working at their desks for nine hours, whose eyes are dry from screens, who look up and find the window has become a slow television broadcasting nothing in particular.

I am watching it now. Or I am going to watch it. The thought of watching is doing some of the work. The actual watching will be less dramatic. It will be a slight turning of the head, a softening of the posture in the chair, the way the shoulders drop when you stop holding the day together. The droplets will arrive at the glass in no particular order, each one a small dark bead that stretches before it lets go and runs down, merging with others, becoming a small river that forks and rejoins. Some will evaporate before they reach the sill. Some will reach the sill and pool there, trembling, before they finally fall off into nothing.

I think about how we talk about time as if it moves in one direction, as if the rain falls and never rises back up into the cloud. But I have stood at the base of a waterfall on a hot day and seen the mist climb, have seen the water go back up into the air in a fine silver spray, and thought: it is not one direction at all. It is a conversation. The water is talking to the stone, to the heat, to the gravity, to the sun. The rain on the window is a conversation between the atmosphere and the glass. Between the sky and my kitchen. Between the year I am in and the year I was in, the one where I was twenty-three and it rained for eleven days straight in a city I no longer remember the name of.

The coffee in the mug is cold. I did not mean to let it go cold. I made it forty minutes ago, sat down, opened the laptop, and then forty minutes happened and the coffee was just *there*, a small dark lake I would have to deal with later. This is the texture of a life lived in the second half of the afternoon. The small deferrals. The coffee that gets cold. The email you meant to send at two that you will send at five, slightly embarrassed, slightly apologetic, as if the four hours in between were your fault and not the fault of the way time pools and thickens when you are not paying attention to it.

Outside, the drizzle has not changed. That is the thing about drizzle. It does not build. It does not crest and break. It simply *is*, the way a hum is, the way the refrigerator hum is, the way your own breathing is when you stop thinking about it. A constant. A background. The world outside the window is going on in its low-resolution way. A neighbor's dog is barking somewhere, three houses down, a short irritated bark followed by a longer one, like it is being talked to. A car passes, its tires making a soft *shhh* on the wet road. A woman in a yellow jacket walks two pigeons ahead of her, one of them stopping to peet at the gutter, the other continuing, and she does not seem to notice the difference, does not seem to need to.

I used to think that noticing things was a kind of waste. That the most efficient way to move through a day was to go from A to B with minimal sensory input, eyes down, ears closed, the whole experience compressed into a single point of arrival. I was twenty-five. I thought this was discipline. I think now it was fear. Not of the rain, not of the pigeon, but of the smallness. Of realizing that a life is not a series of grand arrivals but a series of cold coffees and yellow jackets and dogs barking at something you cannot see. Of realizing that the Tuesday afternoon is not a prelude to something better. It is not a rehearsal. It is the whole thing.

The rain has been falling for an hour now. I can see it in the way the light has changed, the way the street below the window has gone from a warm amber to a soft, flat grey, the way the shadows have lost their edges and become suggestions rather than statements. The world has been watered down. The sharp things are getting soft. The contrast is reducing. And this feels, to me, correct. Like the day is editing itself. Like it is saying, *you do not need all this definition. You can let the edges blur. You can let the coffee be cold and the email be late and the pigeon be where it is.*

There is a woman on the third floor across the street. I can see her in her window, silhouetted, standing still, holding a cup or a glass or just her hands. She is watching the rain too. I do not know if she is lonely or peaceful or just tired. I do not know if she has cold coffee in the kitchen or a warm bath waiting. I do not know if she is thinking about a Tuesday eleven years ago, in a city she will never go back to. But she is here, in the grey light, in the flat sound of water on glass, and she is not the only one. There are others. There are always others, doing the small act of looking at nothing in particular, letting the day be undramatic, letting the rain be just rain.

The drizzle will stop. It will stop the way it started, without announcement, without a clearing, just a thinning, a slowing, a final bead on the glass that does not run. And the light will come back, slightly sharper, the shadows will reassert themselves, the neighbor's dog will stop barking, the car will stop, the woman in the yellow jacket will be gone. And I will look at my laptop, and the cursor will be blinking, patient, waiting for me to type the sentence I have been avoiding, and the coffee will be even colder now, and I will drink it anyway, or I will pour it down the sink, and either way the Tuesday will continue, flat and grey and full of small water, full of the quiet work of being alive on a day that asks nothing of you except that you stay in the chair and let it happen.

And that is enough. That has to be enough. The rain does not need to mean something. The pigeon does not need to be a metaphor. The cold coffee does not need to be a symbol of missed time. It can just be a Tuesday. It can just be the sound. It can just be the watching, and the being watched, and the small, ordinary, unremarkable grace of a day that is no one's story except the one where it happened.

The rain is still falling. I am still here. The cursor is still blinking.

I will drink the coffee.
